title: Filtering Values: filter, take, first, and friends

options.text: Emits 0, 1, 2 then completes and unsubscribes from the interval
Emits 0, 1, 2 but keeps the interval running forever
Emits nothing because interval is infinite

questions.explanation: take(3) emits the first three values and then completes, which tears down the interval — the standard, leak-free way to bound an infinite stream.

questions.prompt: You call `first()` on a stream that completes without emitting any value, and pass no default. What happens?

options.text: The error handler fires with an EmptyError
It silently completes with no emission
It waits forever for a value

questions.explanation: first() (and last()) throw EmptyError when the source is empty and no default is provided. Use a default, or use take(1) to complete without erroring.

questions.prompt: Does `filter` complete the stream when a value fails its predicate?

options.text: No — it just skips non-matching values; the stream completes only when the source does
Yes — the first failing value completes the stream
Yes — filter always completes after the first emission
No — filter never completes under any condition

questions.explanation: filter only removes values. It passes source completion through but does not complete early. Use take/takeWhile/takeUntil to stop a stream.

questions.prompt: Which operators complete the stream early on their own (without waiting for the source to complete)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: take, takeWhile, and first complete once their condition is met. takeLast (and last) can only emit AFTER the source completes, so they never complete an infinite stream.

questions.prompt: To handle exactly one value from a possibly-empty stream WITHOUT risking an EmptyError, use this operator instead of first(). Type it with its argument, e.g. `xxxx(1)`.
questions.explanation: take(1) emits the first value if one exists and simply completes if not — it never throws EmptyError, unlike first().
takeWhile stops at the first value failing the predicate (7). With inclusive: true it emits that boundary value 7 as well before completing, giving 2, 4, 6, 7.
